term: Password hash sync vs. pass-through authentication vs. federation
def: Password hash sync replicates a hash of the on-premises password hash to Entra ID, so sign-in works even if on-premises infrastructure is briefly unavailable. Pass-through authentication validates each sign-in directly against on-premises AD in real time via a lightweight agent, with no password data stored in the cloud. Federation (AD FS) delegates authentication entirely to an on-premises identity provider.
eg: Pass-through authentication needs at least one authentication agent online to work at all, which is a resilience trade-off compared to password hash sync.

def: Conditional Access is a policy engine that evaluates signals (user, device, location, risk) at sign-in time and applies controls in response. MFA is one of the controls Conditional Access can enforce, not a separate policy system of its own.
prompt: Conditional Access is a policy engine that evaluates signals (user, device, location, risk) at sign-in time and applies controls in response. _____ is one of the controls Conditional Access can enforce, not a separate policy system of its own.
eg: A Conditional Access policy could require MFA only for risky sign-ins or unmanaged devices, rather than requiring it for every sign-in unconditionally.

def: Grants just-in-time, time-bound elevation to privileged roles, optionally requiring approval and justification, instead of leaving administrators with standing (always-on) privileged access.
eg: PIM and Conditional Access solve different problems and are commonly layered together, such as requiring MFA (a Conditional Access control) as a condition of activating a PIM-eligible role.

def: Access reviews periodically recertify access that already exists, so an administrator (or the resource owner) confirms it should continue or revokes it. Entitlement management bundles resources into requestable access packages with approval workflows and built-in, automatic expiration for new access.
eg: A scenario about access to time-boxed contractor or project work usually points to entitlement management; a scenario about periodically re-certifying existing standing access points to access reviews.

term: Management groups, subscriptions, and resource groups
def: Management groups group subscriptions so policy and RBAC can be assigned once and inherited down across an organization. Subscriptions are billing and scale boundaries. Resource groups are deployment and lifecycle containers within a subscription.
eg: Management groups don't replace resource groups — they sit above subscriptions in the hierarchy, while resource groups remain the deployment boundary inside each subscription.

term: Azure Policy effects: Deny, Audit, and DeployIfNotExists
def: Deny blocks the creation or update of a noncompliant resource outright. Audit flags noncompliant resources for visibility without blocking anything. DeployIfNotExists automatically remediates by deploying a related resource (like a diagnostic setting) when a required one is missing.
eg: Only DeployIfNotExists and Modify can fix resources that are already noncompliant, and only when a remediation task is run; Audit only reports on them, and Deny only stops new noncompliant ones from being created.

def: A pre-provisioned, governed Azure environment — management group hierarchy, policy, identity, and hub networking — built on the Cloud Adoption Framework, so every new subscription starts from a consistent baseline instead of each team configuring governance independently.
eg: Landing zones are the recommended starting point for any new enterprise Azure environment on the exam, not just a nice-to-have.

term: Log Analytics workspace design: centralized vs. decentralized
def: A centralized workspace simplifies cross-resource queries and gives a single place to see cost and usage, but has coarser access boundaries. Decentralized (per-team or per-subscription) workspaces give finer access control, retention, and data-sovereignty boundaries, at the cost of harder cross-workspace querying.
eg: A regulated subsidiary that needs its own retention and access boundary is a strong signal for a dedicated workspace, even inside an otherwise centralized design.

def: Metrics are lightweight numerical time-series data, well suited to fast, near-real-time alerting on things like CPU or memory thresholds. Logs are structured or free-form records stored in a Log Analytics workspace, queried with KQL, and suited to deep, multi-table investigation.
eg: Reaching for Logs for a simple, fast threshold alert adds unnecessary query latency; reaching for Metrics for a complex correlation query doesn't have the structure to support it.

def: Microsoft's end-to-end guidance for an organization's cloud journey, in seven phases: Strategy, Plan, Ready, Adopt (migrate, modernize, and build workloads), Govern, Secure, and Manage. Azure landing zones are the concrete, deployable implementation of the Ready phase.
eg: CAF is the "why and how to think about it" methodology; a landing zone is the actual environment you get by following it.

def: Microsoft's set of five pillars — reliability, security, cost optimization, operational excellence, and performance efficiency — used to evaluate architectural trade-offs against each other rather than optimizing any one in isolation.
eg: AZ-305 exam scenarios are frequently a trade-off between two of these pillars — recognizing which one the scenario is actually prioritizing is often the real question being asked.

def: The configuration on an Azure resource that routes its platform logs and metrics to a destination — a Log Analytics workspace, storage account, or Event Hub — since resource logs aren't collected anywhere by default until a diagnostic setting sends them there.
eg: This is the missing piece when a resource log type never seems to show up in Azure Monitor anywhere — the resource-level diagnostic setting that would actually emit it hasn't been configured.

def: Enterprise-scale landing zones are deployed and updated as infrastructure as code — Bicep or ARM templates, sometimes Terraform — rather than clicked together in the portal, so the same governed baseline can be redeployed consistently across subscriptions and re-applied whenever the reference architecture changes.
eg: Treating a landing zone's own definition as IaC means a change to policy or hub networking gets tested and versioned like any other code change, instead of being a one-off manual edit to a subscription that already exists.

def: Azure Advisor analyzes your actual resource configuration and usage telemetry, then generates personalized recommendations organized by the same five pillars as the Azure Well-Architected Framework — reliability, security, cost, operational excellence, and performance.
prompt: _____ analyzes your actual resource configuration and usage telemetry, then generates personalized recommendations organized by the same five pillars as the Azure Well-Architected Framework — reliability, security, cost, operational excellence, and performance.
eg: Advisor's recommendations are specific to what's actually deployed and how it's being used, unlike the Azure Well-Architected Framework's pillars themselves, which are general design guidance applied before or during a build.

def: Resource Graph queries resource metadata (type, location, tags, configuration) across many subscriptions at once using a Kusto-like query language, letting an architect audit governance and compliance across management groups, subscriptions, and resource groups without opening each one individually in the portal.
eg: This is read-only inventory and querying — Azure Policy is still the tool that actually enforces or remediates what Resource Graph merely reports on.

def: A system-assigned managed identity is created and tied to the lifecycle of a single resource, deleted automatically when that resource is deleted, and can't be referenced or shared by another resource. A user-assigned managed identity is created as its own standalone resource, can be assigned to many resources at once, and persists independently of any one resource's lifecycle.
eg: A pattern where several VMs or Function Apps all need to authenticate as the same identity to a downstream resource points to a single user-assigned managed identity, not a separate system-assigned identity configured on each one.

def: An initiative groups multiple individual policy definitions into a single assignable unit with a shared set of parameters, so an organization can assign, track compliance for, and manage many related policies — such as tagging, allowed resource types, and encryption requirements — together instead of as separate assignments. The bundled policies can use any mix of effects, such as Deny, Audit, and DeployIfNotExists, within the one assignable set.
eg: Built-in initiatives are commonly what actually get assigned at a management group scope, so a whole bundled set of controls applies consistently to every subscription underneath, rather than assigning 15 separate policies by hand to each one.

def: A small number of cloud-only, non-federated accounts protected by strong, preferably phishing-resistant credentials (such as FIDO2 passkeys or certificate-based authentication), closely monitored, and kept specifically so an administrator can still sign in if a Conditional Access misconfiguration or an MFA outage locks everyone else out. They are the deliberate exception that is typically excluded from the tenant's Conditional Access policies, so those policies can never lock them out.
eg: Excluding these accounts from Conditional Access isn't a security gap — it's the one deliberate exception that keeps the whole tenant from being permanently locked out by its own policies, which is why their own credentials need to be strong and their sign-ins alerted on.

def: Lets a managing tenant, such as a managed service provider or a central IT organization, administer resources in one or more customer tenants directly, through delegated Azure RBAC roles, without the customer's resources ever leaving their own tenant and without the managing tenant needing a separate guest account in each one.
eg: This is the design answer whenever a scenario describes a single team centrally managing resources across multiple, separate Entra ID tenants — Azure Lighthouse delegates access across tenant boundaries, something management groups and plain Azure RBAC can't do on their own, since both are scoped to a single tenant.

term: Custom RBAC roles: Actions, NotActions, and DataActions
def: A custom role definition grants permissions through Actions, the control-plane operations it allows, and can carve out exceptions with NotActions, operations explicitly excluded from what Actions already grants. Data-plane access — reading or writing the data inside a resource, like a blob or a queue message — is governed separately through DataActions, which Actions and NotActions never cover.
eg: A built-in role like Reader can't be edited directly, so a requirement for a role just slightly narrower or broader than any built-in one — including some data-plane access that no existing built-in role quite matches — is the exam's signal to design a custom role instead.

def: A cloud security posture management (CSPM) and workload protection platform that continuously assesses resource configuration against security benchmarks, produces a Secure Score to track improvement over time, and can enable workload-specific threat protection for servers, storage, databases, and more, for active threat detection that goes beyond configuration assessment alone.
eg: Secure Score is a continuously recalculated posture metric derived from actual configuration, which makes it a different kind of signal than Azure Advisor's recommendations — Advisor spans all five Well-Architected pillars, while Defender for Cloud's score is specifically a security-posture measurement.

def: Microsoft's cloud identity and access management service, formerly called Azure Active Directory. It authenticates users, devices, and applications, issues tokens for single sign-on, and is the identity layer behind Azure, Microsoft 365, and thousands of SaaS apps.
eg: It is a separate service from on-premises AD DS, and a hybrid design synchronizes identities into it rather than replacing one with the other. Older exam wording may still say 'Azure AD'.

def: Azure RBAC grants access by assigning a role (a set of allowed actions) to a user, group, or managed identity at a scope: management group, subscription, resource group, or resource. Assignments inherit downward, and a principal's effective access is the sum of all its role assignments.
prompt: Azure _____ grants access by assigning a role (a set of allowed actions) to a user, group, or managed identity at a scope: management group, subscription, resource group, or resource. Assignments inherit downward, and a principal's effective access is the sum of all its role assignments.
eg: Owner, Contributor, and Reader are the broad built-in roles; prefer a narrower built-in role and assign it to a group. RBAC answers 'who can do what', while Azure Policy answers 'what is allowed to exist'.

def: A governance service that evaluates resource properties against rules and either reports compliance or enforces the rule through an effect such as Deny, Audit, Modify, or DeployIfNotExists. Assignments are made at a scope and inherit downward, and remediation tasks can fix existing non-compliant resources.
eg: Policy looks at the state of a resource regardless of who changed it, so it complements RBAC. 'Block creation of VMs outside approved regions' is a Policy requirement, not an RBAC one.

def: A managed service for storing and tightly controlling access to secrets (passwords, connection strings), cryptographic keys, and certificates. Access is governed by Azure RBAC (or older access policies), and soft delete plus purge protection guard against accidental or malicious deletion.
eg: Applications should read secrets at run time using a managed identity instead of embedding credentials in code or config. Customer-managed encryption keys for storage or SQL are typically held in Key Vault. Azure RBAC is the default access model for key vaults created with API version 2026-02-01 and later, and legacy access policies grant vault-wide permissions.

def: A feature of Microsoft Entra External ID that invites external users, such as partners and vendors, to sign in with their own work, school, or social identity. A guest user object is created in your directory so you can assign access and apply Conditional Access to it.
eg: Choose B2B when outside people need your apps or resources but should keep their own credentials, instead of creating and managing separate member accounts for them. Access reviews keep guest access from lingering.

def: A lock protects a resource, resource group, or subscription from accidental change. CanNotDelete lets authorized users read and modify but not delete; ReadOnly blocks changes as well. Locks are inherited by child resources and apply even to Owners until the lock is removed.
eg: Locks only affect control-plane operations. A CanNotDelete lock on a storage account does not stop blobs being deleted through the data plane, so it does not satisfy a data-protection requirement.

def: The platform for collecting, analyzing, and acting on telemetry from Azure and hybrid resources. It stores numeric platform metrics and log data, and drives alerts, dashboards, workbooks, and autoscale from them.
eg: Most monitoring designs use both halves: lightweight metrics for near-real-time alerts, and logs in a Log Analytics workspace for deep KQL investigation and correlation across resources.

def: The data store behind Azure Monitor Logs. A workspace holds tables of log data collected from many sources, queried with Kusto Query Language (KQL), and it is the foundation Microsoft Sentinel is built on. Access can be scoped to the whole workspace or only to resources a user can already reach.
eg: Design questions weigh one central workspace (easier correlation, simpler Sentinel use) against several (data residency, separate retention or billing, delegated access). Retention is set per table.

def: A cloud-native security information and event management (SIEM) and security orchestration, automation, and response (SOAR) service. It ingests logs into a Log Analytics workspace, runs analytics rules to detect threats, and uses automation playbooks to respond to incidents.
eg: Choose Sentinel when a scenario needs threat detection and incident response across many log sources. Defender for Cloud's recommendations and Secure Score cover security posture, which is not the same job.

term: Routing logs: diagnostic setting destinations and Log Analytics table plans
def: A diagnostic setting sends resource logs and metrics to up to three kinds of destination at once: a Log Analytics workspace for querying, a storage account for cheap archive, and an event hub for streaming to a third-party SIEM or other consumer (partner solutions are also supported). Data can be filtered or transformed on the way in with data collection rules. In the workspace, a table's plan (Analytics, Basic, or Auxiliary) sets cost and query capability, and total retention can be extended to 12 years.
eg: Pick the destination from the consumer: query and alert in Azure means a workspace, streaming to Splunk or another SIEM means Event Hubs, and long cold retention means storage or a low-cost table plan.

term: Azure Monitor Agent and data collection rules in a design
def: Azure Monitor Agent is the single supported agent for collecting guest operating system data from Azure VMs, Arc-enabled servers, and scale sets; it replaced the Log Analytics agent, which was retired in August 2024. What it collects, where it sends it, and optional filtering or transformation are defined in data collection rules, which can be shared across many machines and assigned with Azure Policy.
eg: A design that must cut ingestion cost uses a transformation in the rule to drop noisy rows or columns before they are stored.

term: Application Insights for application performance monitoring
def: An Azure Monitor feature for application performance monitoring that collects requests, dependencies, exceptions, and traces from a running application, using OpenTelemetry-based instrumentation where supported. Its data lands in a Log Analytics workspace, and it provides application map, availability tests, live metrics, and distributed tracing across services.
eg: Slow page loads, failing dependencies, and transaction tracing across microservices are Application Insights questions. VM CPU and memory are VM insights questions.

term: Managed Prometheus and Azure Managed Grafana for container monitoring
def: Azure Monitor managed service for Prometheus stores Prometheus metrics from AKS and other clusters without you running Prometheus servers, and Azure Managed Grafana provides managed dashboards over it and over other Azure Monitor data. Container insights collects container logs and inventory into a Log Analytics workspace. Together they cover metrics, dashboards, and logs for Kubernetes.
eg: A team already using PromQL and Grafana dashboards for Kubernetes points to managed Prometheus plus Managed Grafana.

def: Match the signal to the tool: Azure Monitor metrics for fast numeric alerting, Log Analytics for queries across logs, Application Insights for application behavior, VM insights for guest performance and dependencies, Container insights and managed Prometheus for Kubernetes, Network Watcher and Network Insights for network paths, Azure Service Health for platform incidents that affect your subscriptions, and Resource Health for the health of one resource.
eg: Service Health answers 'is Azure having a problem that affects me', and Resource Health answers 'is this one VM unavailable because of the platform'.

def: Publishes on-premises web applications to remote users through Microsoft Entra ID without a VPN or opening inbound firewall ports. A lightweight connector installed on-premises makes only outbound connections to the cloud service, and preauthentication means only requests with a valid token reach the application. Conditional Access and single sign-on apply as for any Entra application.
eg: Microsoft Entra Private Access uses the same connector for non-web and private-network resources.

def: The service for external identities. It covers B2B collaboration for partner and guest users in a workforce tenant, and sign-up and sign-in for customer-facing apps in an external tenant, with a free tier for the first 50,000 monthly active users. Azure AD B2C is no longer available to purchase for new customers since May 1, 2025, so new customer identity designs use External ID.
eg: Existing B2C tenants continue to work. A greenfield consumer-app design should name Microsoft Entra External ID.

term: Lifecycle workflows in Microsoft Entra ID Governance
def: Automate the joiner, mover, and leaver stages of a user's lifecycle: tasks such as generating a temporary access pass, adding to groups or teams, sending notifications, and disabling or removing an account run on triggers like an employee's start date or last day. They sit alongside entitlement management and access reviews in Microsoft Entra ID Governance.
eg: A requirement to automate onboarding and offboarding tasks from HR data points to lifecycle workflows. Periodic recertification points to access reviews.

def: A role assignment can carry a condition that adds a check on attributes of the request, the resource, or the principal, so access is narrower than the role alone. Conditions are currently supported on role assignments with blob or queue data actions, for example to allow Storage Blob Data Reader only on blobs tagged Project=Cascade, or to allow writes only over a private link.
eg: ABAC reduces the number of role assignments and custom roles needed when access depends on tags or other attributes.

def: Azure Key Vault Standard stores software-protected secrets, keys, and certificates, and Premium adds HSM-backed keys. Managed HSM is a fully managed, single-tenant, highly available HSM service using FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated HSMs, for key sovereignty and strict compliance. Azure Cloud HSM is a single-tenant service for lift-and-shift applications that need PKCS#11, JCA, or CNG. Azure Payment HSM supports payment PIN processing.
eg: Customer-managed key scenarios work with Key Vault Standard (software-protected keys); Premium is needed only when the requirement says HSM-protected keys. 'Single tenant' plus 'full control of keys' leads to Managed HSM.

term: Key Vault design: access model, protection, and network
def: Use Azure RBAC for the data plane, which is the default for key vaults created with API version 2026-02-01 and later, and give applications a managed identity rather than stored credentials. Soft delete and purge protection are required for vaults that hold customer-managed keys. Reach the vault over a private endpoint and a firewall, and separate vaults by application, environment, and region to limit the blast radius.
eg: Legacy access policies grant vault-wide permissions. RBAC allows assignments at the vault, or at an individual key, secret, or certificate.

def: A managed service for centrally storing application settings and feature flags, separate from code and shared by many services, regions, and environments. Key-values can use labels for environments and can reference secrets in Key Vault rather than holding them. Dynamic refresh lets applications pick up changes without a restart or redeployment.
eg: App Configuration is for non-secret settings and feature flags. Secrets, keys, and certificates belong in Key Vault.

term: Microsoft Purview vs. Microsoft Defender for Cloud regulatory compliance
def: Microsoft Purview governs data: it catalogs and classifies data across the estate, tracks lineage, and applies sensitivity labels. Defender for Cloud's regulatory compliance dashboard maps the configuration of Azure resources to standards such as ISO 27001, NIST, or PCI DSS using Azure Policy initiatives and lists the failing controls. Azure Policy itself enforces or audits the individual rules.
eg: Questions about discovering and classifying sensitive data are Purview questions. Questions about whether resource configuration meets a standard are Defender for Cloud or Azure Policy questions.

def: Define a small standard set of tags, such as owner, cost center, environment, and application, and enforce it with Azure Policy. Tags are not inherited by default, so a policy with the Modify effect, such as the built-in policy that inherits a tag from the resource group, copies them to resources. Tags drive cost allocation in Cost Management and help find resources with Azure Resource Graph.
eg: A tag requirement stated as 'must be present' is a Deny or Audit policy. 'Applied automatically' is Modify.

term: Azure SQL Database vs. Managed Instance vs. SQL Server on a VM
def: Azure SQL Database (single database) is fully managed PaaS with the least administrative overhead but limited instance-level features. SQL Managed Instance offers near-complete SQL Server engine compatibility (SQL Agent, cross-database queries, linked servers) while staying PaaS. SQL Server on a VM gives full OS and engine control (IaaS) for maximum compatibility, at the cost of managing patching yourself.
eg: A migration that depends on SQL Agent jobs or cross-database queries but still wants to avoid managing the OS points squarely at Managed Instance, not SQL Database.

def: Five levels, from strongest to weakest: Strong, Bounded Staleness, Session, Consistent Prefix, and Eventual. Strong gives no staleness but the highest latency and lowest availability; Eventual gives the lowest latency and highest availability but no ordering guarantee.
eg: Session is the default and fits most single-user scenarios that need to see their own writes immediately; Eventual fits read-heavy workloads (like a shared catalog) that can tolerate a few seconds of staleness in exchange for speed.

def: A good partition key has high cardinality and spreads requests and storage evenly. A low-cardinality key concentrates traffic on a small number of physical partitions, creating a "hot partition" that throttles throughput no matter how much RU/s is provisioned.
eg: The fix for a hot partition is redesigning the partition key itself, not raising the consistency level or adding more provisioned throughput.

term: Storage redundancy: LRS, ZRS, GRS, and GZRS
def: LRS keeps three synchronous copies within one datacenter. ZRS spreads synchronous copies across availability zones in the same region. GRS asynchronously replicates to a paired secondary region (without zone redundancy locally). GZRS combines zone redundancy in the primary region with geo-replication to a secondary region.
eg: Only the "RA-" (read-access) variants of GRS/GZRS let an application read from the secondary region before an actual failover occurs.

term: Access tiers: Hot, Cool, Cold, and Archive
def: Hot suits frequently accessed data at the highest storage cost and lowest access cost. Cool and Cold suit infrequently accessed data, with lower storage cost but higher access cost and longer minimum retention. Archive is the cheapest tier for rarely accessed data, but blobs must be rehydrated (a process that can take hours) before they can be read.
eg: A cost-first requirement with an acceptable multi-hour retrieval delay is the signal for Archive; needing the data readable at any moment rules Archive out even if it's rarely accessed. Archive is also unavailable on ZRS, GZRS, and RA-GZRS accounts.

def: Blob storage with a hierarchical namespace enabled, purpose-built for large-scale analytics (Synapse, Databricks, HDInsight) that need POSIX-like access control lists and efficient directory-level operations, not just flat object storage.
eg: The hierarchical namespace is what turns general-purpose Blob storage into a proper data lake for big-data analytics engines.

term: Data Migration Assistant (DMA) vs. Database Migration Service (DMS)
def: DMA assessed an on-premises database for compatibility issues and deprecated features before any migration happened, but Microsoft retired it on 16 July 2025 and it is no longer available to download. Its assessment role now falls to Azure Migrate (for assessing SQL Server estates at scale) and the SSMS migration component, while Azure Database Migration Service (DMS) performs the actual migration — online (minimal downtime) or offline — into the target Azure data service.
prompt: _____ assessed an on-premises database for compatibility issues and deprecated features before any migration happened, but Microsoft retired it on 16 July 2025 and it is no longer available to download. Its assessment role now falls to Azure Migrate (for assessing SQL Server estates at scale) and the SSMS migration component, while Azure Database Migration Service (_____) performs the actual migration — online (minimal downtime) or offline — into the target Azure data service.
eg: Older material still pairs the two tools: the assessment step ("will this break after we move it?") came from DMA, while DMS is the service that actually moves the data once you're ready to go.

def: A private endpoint gives a PaaS resource a private IP address inside your VNet, reachable privately even from on-premises or peered networks, and can remove its public endpoint entirely. A service endpoint keeps the resource's public IP but optimizes and restricts routing for traffic that already originates from a specific subnet.
eg: Only a private endpoint lets on-premises traffic, arriving over ExpressRoute or a VPN, reach a PaaS service privately — a service endpoint only helps traffic that already starts inside the VNet.

def: Synchronously replicates data across three availability zones within one region, protecting against a datacenter-level failure without the latency or cost of replicating to a second region entirely.
eg: ZRS sits between locally-redundant storage, which only protects against a single rack or disk failure, and the cross-region options that add a paired secondary region.

def: Combines synchronous zone-redundant replication across availability zones in the primary region with asynchronous replication to a second, paired region — protecting against both a zone failure and a full regional outage in one redundancy setting.
eg: Of LRS, ZRS, GRS, and GZRS, this is the strongest option for a design that must survive a regional outage without giving up the zone-level durability that ZRS already provides day to day.

def: A rule-based policy on a storage account that automatically moves blobs down through the Hot, Cool, Cold, and Archive access tiers as they age, and deletes them once a defined retention period ends, all without anyone manually re-tiering or cleaning up data by hand. This is what actually enforces a cost-driven tiering strategy over time, rather than a one-time manual tier assignment made only at upload.
eg: A lifecycle policy is what actually delivers on the cost promise of Archive tier in practice — without one, data that should have aged into a cheaper tier months ago just sits in Hot, quietly costing more than it needs to.

term: Cosmos DB APIs: NoSQL, MongoDB, Cassandra, Gremlin, and Table
def: Cosmos DB is a multi-model service, and the API chosen determines the data model and drivers an application uses: Core (SQL), now branded the API for NoSQL, for native JSON documents with SQL-like queries, MongoDB for wire-protocol compatibility with existing MongoDB apps, Cassandra for existing Cassandra workloads, Gremlin for graph data and traversal queries, and Table for a premium, higher-scale replacement for Azure Table storage. Consistency levels and partition key design apply the same way no matter which API is chosen.
eg: Picking the API isn't just a syntax preference — it's what lets an existing MongoDB or Cassandra application move to Cosmos DB with minimal code changes, since the wire protocol stays compatible.

term: Azure Database for PostgreSQL / MySQL Flexible Server
def: Fully managed, open-source relational database hosting with built-in high availability (zone-redundant or same-zone), granular control over maintenance windows, and lower cost than the older Single Server deployment option, which Microsoft has retired (PostgreSQL Single Server on 28 March 2025 and MySQL Single Server on 16 September 2024). It is the hosting choice for open-source engines, much as Azure SQL Database, Managed Instance, or SQL Server on a VM are the choices for SQL Server.
eg: This is the answer whenever a scenario needs to migrate an existing PostgreSQL or MySQL application to Azure while keeping the same open-source engine, rather than rewriting it against Azure SQL Database or Cosmos DB.

def: A time-based immutability policy enforces write-once, read-many (WORM) protection on blobs, preventing modification or deletion until a set retention period elapses. In locked mode, not even an account administrator can shorten the retention period or remove the policy before it expires. This is a stronger, prevention-based guarantee than a lifecycle management policy, which only automates tiering and deletion over time rather than blocking either outright.
prompt: A time-based immutability policy enforces write-once, read-many (_____) protection on blobs, preventing modification or deletion until a set retention period elapses. In locked mode, not even an account administrator can shorten the retention period or remove the policy before it expires. This is a stronger, prevention-based guarantee than a lifecycle management policy, which only automates tiering and deletion over time rather than blocking either outright.
eg: A regulatory requirement that data be genuinely undeletable until a retention period ends calls for a locked immutability policy specifically, not just soft delete, which still permits eventual deletion.

term: Azure Synapse Analytics: serverless vs. dedicated SQL pools
def: A serverless SQL pool bills per query based on the data actually processed, with no compute to provision or pay for while idle, suited to ad hoc or unpredictable querying. A dedicated SQL pool pre-allocates provisioned compute measured in DWUs, suited to sustained, predictable, high-performance workloads. Serverless pools commonly query files sitting directly in Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 without first loading them into a database.
eg: Choosing dedicated for infrequent, ad hoc analytics means paying for idle provisioned compute; choosing serverless for a constant, heavy workload can end up costing more per query than a dedicated pool would have.

term: Azure SQL Database purchasing models: DTU vs. vCore, and Hyperscale
def: The DTU-based model bundles compute, memory, and storage I/O into a single blended unit, simple to budget but hard to scale any one dimension independently. The vCore model prices compute and storage separately, maps directly to physical cores and memory (easing on-premises core-license comparisons), and is the only model that offers the Hyperscale service tier, which can scale storage up to 128 TB with near-instant backups and fast scale-out using read replicas.
eg: Hyperscale decouples storage growth from compute size entirely, which is the detail that matters when a scenario describes a database that needs to grow far beyond what a fixed DTU tier or a General Purpose/Business Critical vCore tier can comfortably hold.

term: Cosmos DB throughput: provisioned vs. serverless capacity mode
def: Provisioned throughput (standard or autoscale) reserves RU/s capacity ahead of time so performance is predictable, suited to steady or predictable workloads. Serverless capacity mode bills per request unit actually consumed, with no RU/s to provision or pay for while idle, suited to spiky or low-traffic workloads where paying for always-on capacity would waste money.
eg: Autoscale, within provisioned mode, still reserves a maximum RU/s ceiling and scales automatically between a floor and that ceiling; serverless goes further and removes the need to provision any RU/s at all, but it caps total storage per container and isn't available alongside multi-region writes.

term: Azure Data Factory vs. Synapse pipelines for data integration
def: Azure Data Factory is a standalone, code-free ETL/ELT orchestration service for moving and transforming data across on-premises and cloud sources with a large library of connectors. Synapse pipelines provide that same underlying pipeline engine and designer experience, but built directly inside Azure Synapse Analytics, alongside its serverless and dedicated SQL pools and Spark pools in one unified workspace.
eg: Choosing Synapse pipelines over a standalone Data Factory instance is mainly about workspace consolidation — keeping ingestion, transformation, and querying together in one Synapse workspace — rather than a difference in the underlying orchestration capability itself.

def: Azure Cosmos DB is a globally distributed, fully managed NoSQL database with SLA-backed low latency, turnkey multi-region replication, and a choice of APIs. Throughput is measured in Request Units, and data is spread across partitions by a partition key.
prompt: Azure _____ is a globally distributed, fully managed NoSQL database with SLA-backed low latency, turnkey multi-region replication, and a choice of APIs. Throughput is measured in Request Units, and data is spread across partitions by a partition key.
eg: Pick it for globally distributed, low-latency, schema-flexible workloads that must scale writes horizontally. Pick Azure SQL for relational data that needs joins and multi-table transactions.

def: The normalized currency for Cosmos DB throughput, rolling CPU, memory, and IOPS into one number. A point read of a 1 KB item by ID and partition key costs 1 RU; larger items, writes, and queries cost more. Requests beyond the provisioned RU/s are throttled with HTTP 429.
eg: To size or price a Cosmos DB design, estimate RUs per operation times operations per second. Strong and bounded staleness consistency roughly double the RU cost of reads.

def: Keeps three synchronous copies of your data within a single datacenter in the primary region. It is the cheapest redundancy option and protects against disk and rack failures, but not against a datacenter or availability zone outage.
eg: LRS suits data that is easy to recreate or must stay inside one datacenter for compliance. Any requirement to survive a zone failure eliminates it.

def: Keeps three synchronous copies in the primary region, then asynchronously copies the data to a single location in the paired secondary region, where it is stored with LRS again. The secondary copy is not readable unless you use RA-GRS, and it is used only after a failover.
prompt: Keeps three synchronous copies in the primary region, then asynchronously copies the data to a single location in the paired secondary region, where it is stored with LRS again. The secondary copy is not readable unless you use RA-_____, and it is used only after a failover.
eg: Replication is asynchronous, so a failover can lose the most recent writes. GRS fits a requirement to survive a regional outage with a non-zero RPO, never an RPO of zero.

def: GRS with read access to the secondary region enabled. The secondary copy can be read at any time through a separate endpoint (the account name with -secondary appended), without waiting for a failover.
eg: It suits read-only reporting or apps that keep reading during a primary-region outage. The secondary can lag behind the primary because replication is asynchronous.

def: GZRS with read access to the secondary region enabled. The primary stores data across three availability zones, and the secondary copy in the paired region can be read through the -secondary endpoint at any time.
eg: Pick it when a design needs both zone-failure tolerance and read availability during a regional outage, for example a customer-facing app that must keep serving reads.

def: Keeps deleted or overwritten blobs, snapshots, and versions recoverable for a retention period of 1 to 365 days instead of removing them immediately. It protects individual blobs only: it cannot recover blobs once their container or the storage account is deleted.
eg: Pair it with container soft delete when whole containers might be deleted by mistake. For protection against tampering, use immutability policies, since soft-deleted data eventually expires.

def: Keeps a deleted container and all the blobs in it recoverable for a retention period (default 7 days, range 1 to 365). It is a separate setting from blob soft delete, which cannot restore blobs after their parent container is deleted.
eg: A classic scenario: an admin deletes a container, blob soft delete was on, yet nothing can be restored. Container soft delete is the missing feature.

def: Automatically keeps the previous version of a blob each time it is overwritten or deleted, so any earlier version can be read or restored by its version ID. Versions accrue storage cost until you delete them or a lifecycle rule does.
eg: Versioning protects against overwrites as well as deletes, and Microsoft recommends enabling it together with soft delete. Add a lifecycle rule to expire old versions and control cost.

def: A group of Azure SQL databases that share one pool of compute (eDTUs or vCores) at a single price. Each database can use what it needs within configured minimum and maximum limits, so pools save money when many databases have low average use with spikes at different times.
eg: A typical case is a SaaS app with hundreds of tenant databases whose peaks rarely overlap. A pool is cheaper than sizing every database for its own peak.

term: Azure SQL data protection features and what each protects against
def: Transparent data encryption encrypts database files and backups at rest and is on by default. Always Encrypted encrypts sensitive columns on the client so that even administrators cannot see plaintext in the database, and secure enclaves enable richer queries over it. Dynamic data masking hides values from non-privileged users in query results without changing stored data. Row-level security filters which rows a user can see. Ledger makes changes tamper-evident, and Microsoft Defender for SQL detects threats and vulnerabilities.
eg: Match the threat: stolen files means TDE, an untrusted administrator means Always Encrypted, a support agent seeing too much means masking or row-level security, and proving data was not altered means ledger.

def: Hyperscale supports databases up to 128 TB with storage that grows automatically, snapshot-based backups that do not burden compute, and fast scaling of compute without moving data. It provides built-in high-availability replicas, up to 30 named replicas with independent compute for read workloads, and geo-replicas. It is available only in the vCore purchasing model and supports serverless compute.
eg: A very large database with fast backups, many read replicas, and unchanged T-SQL points to Hyperscale.

term: Provisioned vs. serverless compute in Azure SQL Database
def: Provisioned compute reserves a fixed number of vCores and bills for them continuously, which suits steady workloads. Serverless scales compute automatically between a configured minimum and maximum number of vCores and bills per second for what is used; in the General Purpose tier it can also pause automatically when the database is idle, so only storage is billed.
eg: Intermittent, unpredictable, or development workloads suit serverless. A database that must respond instantly after idle time may prefer provisioned compute, because resuming from a pause takes time.

term: Scaling relational data: elastic pools, read scale-out, and sharding
def: An elastic pool shares a set of resources among many single databases whose peaks occur at different times, which suits SaaS with many tenant databases. Read scale-out sends read-only queries to a built-in secondary replica in the Premium, Business Critical, and Hyperscale tiers. When one database outgrows a single node, sharding splits data across databases using the elastic database tools. Hyperscale adds independently scaled named replicas.
eg: Many small databases with uneven load point to an elastic pool. One database too big or too busy for one node points to Hyperscale or sharding.

def: The Managed Instance link uses distributed availability groups to replicate data in near real time between SQL Server (hosted anywhere) and Azure SQL Managed Instance. It supports offloading read-only workloads and analytics to Azure, migrating with minimal downtime, and, with SQL Server 2022 and later, disaster recovery with fail back to SQL Server.
eg: Near real-time replication from on-premises SQL Server to a managed instance, with the option to fail back, is the signal for the link feature.

term: Azure Cosmos DB vector search and fabric mirroring
def: Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL can store vector embeddings next to the operational JSON documents and run vector similarity queries with flat, quantized flat, or DiskANN indexes, so an AI application can use one database for both. Data can also be mirrored into Microsoft Fabric for analytics without building pipelines.
eg: A retrieval-augmented generation app that already keeps its documents in Cosmos DB does not need a separate vector database.

term: Choosing storage for unstructured and file data
def: Blob Storage holds objects and backs Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 when the hierarchical namespace is on. Azure Files provides managed SMB and NFS shares. Azure NetApp Files provides high-performance enterprise NFS, SMB, and dual-protocol volumes with five service levels (Elastic, Flexible, Standard, Premium, and Ultra). Azure Elastic SAN provides pooled block storage reached over iSCSI. Managed disks give block storage to a single VM or a cluster using shared disks.
eg: Choose by access pattern: objects over an API, a mounted file share, a high-performance enterprise file system, or pooled block storage.

def: A first-party, fully managed file storage service built on NetApp technology, offering NFS (v3 and v4.1), SMB, and dual-protocol volumes with low latency at the higher service levels, snapshots, cross-region replication, and volumes sized by capacity pool quota. It targets enterprise file workloads such as SAP, HPC, and lift-and-shift of NAS applications.
eg: Look for requirements such as migrating NetApp workloads, very low latency for file access, or enterprise NAS features that Azure Files does not match.

def: A managed storage area network service that lets you provision one SAN with pooled capacity and performance and carve it into volumes that connect over iSCSI to many compute resources, including VMs, AKS, and Azure VMware Solution. You scale base capacity, IOPS, and throughput of the SAN as a whole rather than per disk.
eg: A requirement to consolidate block storage for many workloads under one pooled, scalable resource points to Elastic SAN rather than separately sized managed disks.

def: A unified software-as-a-service analytics platform that brings data engineering, data integration (Data Factory), data warehousing, real-time intelligence, data science, and Power BI into one workspace on OneLake, a single logical data lake for the whole organization. Shortcuts reference data in other locations without copying it, and Fabric items store data in open Delta Parquet format.
eg: A design that wants one governed platform for ingest, lake, warehouse, and reporting, with little infrastructure to manage, points to Fabric.

term: Choosing a data analysis platform: Fabric, Databricks, and Synapse
def: Microsoft Fabric is the integrated SaaS analytics platform. Azure Databricks is a Spark-based platform for data engineering and machine learning with notebooks, Delta Lake, and a rich ecosystem, and teams often keep it for existing Spark workloads. Azure Synapse Analytics is the earlier analytics service with dedicated and serverless SQL pools and Spark pools, still available for existing solutions.
eg: A new analytics estate with low operational overhead leans to Fabric. An existing Spark and MLOps investment leans to Databricks.

term: Azure Stream Analytics vs. Event Hubs vs. Fabric Real-Time Intelligence
def: Event Hubs ingests and buffers high-volume event streams. Azure Stream Analytics is a fully managed engine that runs continuous SQL-like queries, with time windows, over streams from Event Hubs or IoT Hub and writes results to stores such as SQL Database, Power BI, or Blob Storage. Real-Time Intelligence in Microsoft Fabric provides event streams and real-time analytics inside the Fabric platform.
eg: Ingestion is Event Hubs, continuous processing is Stream Analytics, and storing the results for later analysis is a different service again.

term: Balancing storage features, performance, and cost
def: Cost levers for Azure Storage include the redundancy level, the access tier (Hot, Cool, Cold, Archive), lifecycle management that moves data between tiers automatically, reserved capacity for predictable volumes (a one-year or three-year commitment), and Standard or Premium performance. Premium block blob accounts, Premium file shares, and Ultra or Premium SSD v2 disks buy low latency and high IOPS at higher cost.
eg: A workload with a long-lived, predictable footprint adds reserved capacity. A data set with decaying access adds lifecycle rules.

def: Azure Storage designs for at least 11 nines of durability over a year with locally redundant storage, at least 12 nines with zone-redundant storage, and at least 16 nines with geo-redundant or geo-zone-redundant storage. Durability is about not losing data, while availability, and an SLA, is about being able to read and write it, so read-access variants add availability from the secondary region.
eg: A requirement for the highest durability and protection against a regional loss points to GRS or GZRS. Surviving a zone failure alone needs only ZRS.

term: Azure Backup vs. Azure Site Recovery
def: Azure Backup protects data, restoring files, VMs, or databases to a prior point in time. Azure Site Recovery protects availability, replicating an entire VM or workload to a secondary region or zone so it can fail over and keep running through an outage.
eg: A request to recover an accidentally deleted file points to Backup; a request to keep an application running after a regional outage points to Site Recovery.

def: Availability zones give synchronous, low-latency redundancy across physically separate datacenters within one region, protecting against a single-datacenter loss. A secondary region provides asynchronous DR redundancy against a full regional disaster, at the cost of higher replication latency.
eg: Zones and a secondary region solve two different failure scopes, and a well-designed solution frequently uses both together rather than choosing one over the other.

def: Group one or more databases on a logical server, replicate them to a secondary region, and expose stable read-write and read-only listener endpoints that automatically redirect after a failover, so application connection strings never need to change.
eg: The read-only listener can serve reads from the secondary region even before any failover occurs, not only afterward.

term: Designing from RTO and RPO targets
def: Business requirements set the maximum tolerable downtime and the maximum tolerable data loss first. The backup frequency, replication approach, and failover automation are then designed to meet those targets, rather than being chosen first and having the numbers backfilled to match.
eg: A design question that states specific RTO/RPO numbers is really asking you to pick the cheapest architecture that still satisfies both, not the most impressive-sounding one.

def: The container that stores Azure Backup data and Azure Site Recovery replication configuration and metadata. A single vault can hold both backup and Site Recovery items. The vault's own storage redundancy setting (locally redundant, geo-redundant, or zone-redundant) determines whether it survives a regional loss: only geo-redundant storage keeps a copy in another region.
eg: It's easy to assume backups automatically survive a regional outage — that depends entirely on the vault's own storage redundancy setting, which is worth checking explicitly.

def: Active-active runs full production traffic in two or more regions simultaneously, giving the fastest possible RTO at the highest cost and complexity (including handling multi-region write conflicts). Active-passive keeps a warm or cold standby region that only takes traffic after a failover, which is cheaper but slower to recover.
eg: "Zero perceptible downtime during a regional failure" is the signal phrase for active-active; any standby that needs to be activated first, warm or cold, is active-passive.

term: Availability sets: fault domains and update domains
def: An availability set spreads VMs across fault domains (separate physical racks with independent power and network, protecting against hardware failure) and update domains (groups that Azure patches and reboots at different times, protecting against planned maintenance), all within a single datacenter. This is a narrower scope of protection than availability zones or a paired secondary region: it covers rack-level and maintenance-level failure inside one datacenter, not the loss of the datacenter itself.
eg: An availability set is the lighter-weight, single-datacenter alternative to spreading VMs across availability zones, worth reaching for when a scenario explicitly doesn't need datacenter-level protection.

def: When a workload chains multiple dependent Azure services together, its overall availability is the product of each service's individual SLA, not the lowest single SLA in the chain — combining two services each rated at 99.9% actually yields a composite SLA below 99.9%, unless a redundant path is added to compensate. This is a concrete, calculable input to the reliability pillar of the Azure Well-Architected Framework, not just an abstract design goal.
prompt: When a workload chains multiple dependent Azure services together, its overall availability is the product of each service's individual SLA, not the lowest single SLA in the chain — combining two services each rated at 99.9% actually yields a _____ below 99.9%, unless a redundant path is added to compensate. This is a concrete, calculable input to the reliability pillar of the Azure Well-Architected Framework, not just an abstract design goal.
eg: This is why a design with several chained dependencies often needs redundant paths through some of those services — otherwise the composite math can quietly fall short of a stated availability target even when every individual service meets its own SLA.

def: A common backup retention design that keeps daily backups (son) for a short window, weekly backups (father) for a medium window, and monthly or yearly backups (grandfather) for the longest window, balancing storage cost against how far back a restore point needs to reach. This retention design is configured on an Azure Backup policy, not on Azure Site Recovery's replication settings.
eg: Azure Backup policies implement this by letting daily, weekly, monthly, and yearly retention rules be configured independently on the same policy, rather than keeping every daily recovery point forever.

def: Spins up recovered VMs in an isolated network specifically to validate that replicated data is recoverable, without touching production traffic or the live replication itself. This is a feature of Azure Site Recovery specifically, not of Azure Backup.
eg: Running the test into an isolated virtual network, not the production VNet, avoids IP address and naming conflicts with the still-running primary VMs during the drill.

def: A fault-injection testing service that deliberately triggers failures — killing a VM, injecting network latency, throttling a dependency — against a running Azure environment, so a team can observe and validate how a workload's actual resiliency design behaves under real failure conditions, rather than only on paper.
eg: This complements, rather than replaces, Azure Site Recovery test failover: Chaos Studio validates how a live, running architecture tolerates and recovers from in-place faults, while a Site Recovery test failover specifically validates that replicated data in a secondary location is recoverable.

term: Cosmos DB multi-region failover priority and write-conflict resolution
def: With multiple read regions configured, an account's failover priority list determines which region Cosmos DB promotes to primary if the current write region fails, and automatic failover follows that list without manual intervention unless it's disabled. If multi-region writes are enabled instead, concurrent writes to the same item in different regions are resolved automatically, by last-writer-wins based on a timestamp, unless a custom conflict resolution policy is defined.
eg: A requirement that conflicting writes be resolved by specific business logic, rather than simply keeping whichever write has the latest timestamp, is the signal to configure a custom conflict resolution policy instead of relying on the default last-writer-wins behavior.

def: Lets an administrator manually trigger an unplanned failover of a GRS, GZRS, RA-GRS, or RA-GZRS storage account, promoting the secondary region to primary during a real outage. After the failover, the account temporarily becomes locally redundant in the new primary region until geo-redundancy is explicitly reconfigured, and any writes that hadn't yet replicated to the secondary before the failover are lost.
eg: This is a deliberate, administrator-triggered action for a genuine regional outage, not something Azure performs automatically on its own — a design that assumes failover happens by itself without anyone initiating it is assuming a behavior the feature doesn't actually provide.

term: Azure Site Recovery recovery points: app-consistent vs. crash-consistent
def: A crash-consistent recovery point captures disk data as if the VM had simply lost power, with no guarantee that in-memory or in-flight application transactions were flushed to disk first. An app-consistent recovery point additionally quiesces the application before the snapshot, guaranteeing that in-flight transactions are captured cleanly, at the cost of being taken less frequently than crash-consistent points.
eg: A database workload that can't tolerate a failover point that might land mid-transaction is the scenario that calls for app-consistent recovery points specifically, even though they're captured on a longer interval than crash-consistent points.

term: Traffic Manager routing methods: Priority, Weighted, Performance, and Geographic
def: Priority routing sends all traffic to the highest-priority healthy endpoint, falling back to the next one only on failure — the method that actually implements an active-passive multi-region design at the DNS layer. Weighted distributes traffic across endpoints by a configured ratio, useful for a gradual rollout. Performance routes to whichever endpoint has the lowest network latency for the requester. Geographic routes based on the requester's geographic location, often to satisfy data-residency requirements.
eg: Picking Priority for what's actually meant to be an active-active multi-region design would quietly turn the backup regions into idle, untested capacity — Performance or Weighted across every region is what an active-active design actually calls for at the DNS layer.

def: An Azure SQL Database feature that asynchronously replicates a single database to up to four readable secondary databases in the same or other regions. Failover is initiated per database, and each failover changes which server is primary.
eg: Choose it for per-database control or extra read replicas. Choose auto-failover groups when several databases must fail over together behind stable listener endpoints that keep connection strings unchanged.

def: Azure SQL automatic backups let you restore a database to any moment within the retention window, which defaults to 7 days and can be set from 1 to 35 days (1 to 7 for the Basic tier). The restore creates a new database rather than overwriting the original.
eg: PITR fixes accidental deletes or bad updates. Keeping backups beyond 35 days needs long-term retention, which can hold full backups for up to 10 years.

def: A disaster-recovery option that restores an Azure SQL database from geo-replicated backups onto any server in any Azure region. It is available only when backup storage is geo-redundant (GRS or GZRS).
eg: It is the cheapest SQL DR option because no standby replica runs, but recovery is slower and can lose more data. If the stem needs fast failover with a stable connection string, choose a failover group instead.

def: A recovery plan organizes machines into ordered groups so a multi-tier application fails over in sequence: machines in a group start in parallel, and groups start in order. It can also include manual actions and Azure Automation runbooks.
prompt: A _____ organizes machines into ordered groups so a multi-tier application fails over in sequence: machines in a group start in parallel, and groups start in order. It can also include manual actions and Azure Automation runbooks.
eg: Use one so the database tier is up before the app and web tiers, and to automate steps such as attaching public IPs. Run test failovers with the plan and repeat them as the application changes.

def: An Azure Backup option for Recovery Services vaults that use geo-redundant storage. With it enabled, backed-up VMs and databases can be restored in the paired secondary region at any time, not only after a regional outage.
eg: It is useful for audit and compliance DR drills and for restoring during an outage. Secondary-region recovery points can lag the primary because the backup data replicates asynchronously.

term: Backup and recovery for compute workloads
def: Azure Backup protects Azure VMs with snapshots plus a copy in a Recovery Services vault, and protects SQL Server and SAP HANA databases running in VMs with workload-aware backups. On-premises servers use the MARS agent, Azure Backup Server, or System Center DPM. For VM, scale set, and hybrid workloads that must resume within a tight recovery time objective rather than restore from a backup, Azure Site Recovery replication is the better fit.
eg: Backup answers 'restore an earlier copy'. Site Recovery answers 'run the workload somewhere else, soon'.

def: Azure SQL Database takes automated backups with point-in-time restore, kept for 7 days by default and configurable from 1 to 35 days, and long-term retention can keep full backups for up to 10 years. Azure Cosmos DB offers periodic backup, or continuous backup with point-in-time restore within a 7-, 30-, or 35-day tier. SQL Server in a VM uses Azure Backup's workload backup, and flexible server databases keep their own automated backups.
eg: 'Restore to any point in the last N days' points to point-in-time restore or continuous backup. 'Keep yearly copies for seven years' points to long-term retention.

term: Backup and recovery for unstructured data: Blob Storage and Azure Files
def: For blobs, operational backup is continuous, keeps changes inside the source storage account, and restores to a point in time; vaulted backup copies data to a Backup vault in a separate, Microsoft-managed location, protecting against account deletion or malicious deletion. Azure Files can be backed up through a Recovery Services vault using snapshot backups, or with the vaulted tier that copies data out of the storage account.
eg: A requirement to survive deletion of the whole storage account rules out options that keep the data only inside that account, such as soft delete, versioning, snapshots, and operational backup.

term: Protecting backups from ransomware and insider deletion
def: An immutable vault blocks operations that could lead to the loss of recovery points, and locking the setting makes it irreversible. Soft delete retains deleted backup data, and enhanced soft delete makes the retention period configurable and can be made always on. Multi-user authorization uses a Resource Guard, owned by a separate team or in another subscription or tenant, so critical operations need a second approver. Cross Region Restore lets you restore from the paired region.
eg: A compromised backup administrator is the threat model behind immutability, enhanced soft delete, and Resource Guard.

term: Azure Site Recovery for Azure, on-premises, and other workloads
def: Site Recovery replicates Azure VMs between regions, on-premises VMware VMs, Hyper-V VMs, and physical servers to Azure, and Windows instances from AWS to Azure. Failover is orchestrated with recovery plans that order the start-up of tiers and add scripts or manual steps, and a test failover validates the plan in an isolated network without affecting production.
eg: A hybrid disaster recovery requirement with a minutes-level recovery time and no secondary datacenter to build points to Site Recovery with Azure as the target.

term: High availability for compute: SLAs and placement
def: Two or more VMs spread across availability zones qualify for a 99.99 percent SLA, VMs in an availability set within one datacenter for 99.95 percent, and a single VM with premium storage for 99.9 percent. Virtual Machine Scale Sets spread instances across zones and fault domains automatically. In front of them, zone-redundant load balancers and application gateways keep the entry point available when a zone fails.
eg: Zones protect against a datacenter failure. Availability sets protect against a rack or host failure inside one datacenter. Neither protects against a regional outage.

def: Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance can be zone-redundant so that a zone failure is handled by automatic failover inside the region with no application change, while auto-failover groups add a regional secondary with a single listener endpoint. PostgreSQL and MySQL flexible servers offer zone-redundant high availability with a synchronously replicated standby in another zone. SQL Server on VMs uses Always On availability groups across zones.
eg: Zone redundancy answers a datacenter failure inside a region. A failover group answers the loss of the entire region.

term: High availability for semi-structured and unstructured data
def: Zone-redundant storage keeps data available through a zone failure, and geo-zone-redundant storage adds a secondary region, with the read-access variants allowing reads from it. Azure Files and managed disks support zone-redundant options. Azure Cosmos DB can be deployed across availability zones and across regions with multi-region writes and automatic failover priorities.
eg: Cosmos DB availability is configured by adding regions and zones to the account, and the consistency level chosen affects what multi-region writes allow.

def: The global tier of Azure Load Balancer places one static anycast public IP address in front of regional Standard public load balancers. Traffic goes to the closest healthy regional deployment using geo-proximity routing, and fails over to the next best region if one becomes unhealthy. It works at layer 4 for TCP and UDP and preserves the client IP address.
eg: For HTTP applications that need path routing, caching, or WAF, Azure Front Door is the global choice; for any TCP or UDP traffic, the global load balancer fits.

def: Resiliency in Azure, the new name of the Azure Business Continuity Center, is a unified place to manage the resilience posture of the whole estate: backup and disaster recovery protection across Azure Backup and Site Recovery, zone resiliency, and ransomware protection. It shows protected and unprotected resources across subscriptions in one view.
prompt: _____, the new name of the Azure Business Continuity Center, is a unified place to manage the resilience posture of the whole estate: backup and disaster recovery protection across Azure Backup and Site Recovery, zone resiliency, and ransomware protection. It shows protected and unprotected resources across subscriptions in one view.
eg: Older material may say Business Continuity Center or Backup center. Backup center is the legacy experience that it replaced.

term: Choosing compute: VM vs. App Service vs. AKS vs. Container Apps vs. Functions
def: VMs give full OS control for legacy or specialized workloads. App Service is managed PaaS web hosting with no orchestration to manage. AKS gives full Kubernetes control for complex microservices needing custom orchestration. Container Apps runs serverless containers with built-in autoscaling and microservices features, without managing a cluster. Functions is event-driven, per-execution billed compute for short-lived triggered code.
eg: "Wants container-based autoscaling but doesn't want to manage a cluster" is the classic signal for Container Apps over AKS.

def: A central hub VNet hosts shared services — firewall, VPN or ExpressRoute gateway, DNS — while spoke VNets (one per workload or team) peer only to the hub, not to each other, centralizing connectivity, inspection, and cost.
eg: By default, peering to a shared hub does not let two spokes talk to each other directly — that isolation is often the whole point of the design. An Azure landing zone typically ships this topology already built for new workloads to land into.

term: VNet peering vs. VPN Gateway vs. ExpressRoute
def: VNet peering connects Azure VNets directly over Microsoft's backbone, with low latency and no gateway required. A Site-to-Site VPN Gateway connects on-premises networks to Azure over an encrypted tunnel across the public internet. ExpressRoute is a private, dedicated circuit to Azure through a connectivity provider, bypassing the public internet for higher, more predictable bandwidth.
eg: ExpressRoute is the answer whenever a scenario needs the most predictable bandwidth and latency and is willing to work with a connectivity provider for a dedicated circuit.

term: Azure Front Door vs. Application Gateway vs. Traffic Manager
def: Front Door is a global, layer-7 entry point with edge caching, a Web Application Firewall, and routing across regions. Application Gateway is a regional layer-7 load balancer that can also provide a Web Application Firewall, but only within one region. Traffic Manager is DNS-based global routing with no data-plane inspection — it only returns which endpoint's IP address to use.
eg: Because Traffic Manager works purely at the DNS layer, its failover is limited by client-side DNS caching (TTL), unlike Front Door's real data-plane failover.

term: Network security group (NSG) vs. Azure Firewall
def: An NSG is a per-subnet or per-NIC allow/deny filter on IP address, port, and protocol — simple and free. Azure Firewall is a managed, stateful, centralized firewall supporting FQDN-based filtering and unified logging across many VNets, suited to enforcing a perimeter from a hub.
prompt: An _____ is a per-subnet or per-NIC allow/deny filter on IP address, port, and protocol — simple and free. Azure Firewall is a managed, stateful, centralized firewall supporting FQDN-based filtering and unified logging across many VNets, suited to enforcing a perimeter from a hub.
eg: NSGs have no concept of a fully qualified domain name — FQDN-based outbound filtering across a whole hub-and-spoke estate calls for Azure Firewall, not a pile of per-subnet NSGs.

def: The hub service for discovering on-premises servers and workloads and assessing them (right-sizing, readiness, cost estimation) before any workload is moved, and for coordinating the migration tools that then carry out the move.
eg: Azure Migrate is the answer for the discovery-and-assessment phase; the actual move is done by its integrated migration tools or handed off to a more specialized tool like Azure Database Migration Service.

term: Service Bus vs. Event Grid vs. Event Hubs
def: Service Bus is a message broker for ordered, transactional, point-to-point or pub/sub messaging with guaranteed delivery. Event Grid is a lightweight, reactive eventing service for discrete event notifications with push-based routing. Event Hubs is built for high-throughput streaming and telemetry ingestion at massive scale.
eg: A requirement for reliable, ordered, exactly-processed order queues points to Service Bus; a requirement to react to "a blob was created" points to Event Grid; high-volume telemetry ingestion points to Event Hubs.

def: A facade placed in front of backend APIs, regardless of where or how they're hosted, adding a consistent gateway for authentication, rate limiting, versioning, and a developer portal, decoupling API consumers from the underlying implementation.
eg: API Management is the answer whenever multiple differently-hosted backends need one consistent, versioned, authenticated surface for external or partner consumers.

term: Logic Apps vs. Azure Functions for integration
def: Logic Apps is a low-code, designer-driven workflow orchestrator with hundreds of prebuilt connectors, suited to integrating SaaS and enterprise systems. Azure Functions is code-first, event-triggered compute, better suited when custom logic or fine-grained execution control is the priority.
eg: A requirement that business analysts, not just developers, be able to understand and adjust the flow is a strong signal for Logic Apps over hand-written Functions code.

def: A Microsoft-managed networking service that automates large-scale hub-and-spoke connectivity — branch, VPN, and ExpressRoute connections, hubs, and routing — across many regions, instead of building and peering each hub manually.
eg: Virtual WAN is the answer when a design needs to scale hub-and-spoke connectivity across many regions without hand-configuring peering and routing for every hub.

term: Scale up vs. scale out for App Service
def: Scaling up changes the App Service plan's pricing tier or size to a bigger instance. Scaling out adds more instances of the same tier, often automated through autoscale rules based on metrics or a schedule.
eg: Autoscale rules configure scaling out (more instances); changing to a larger tier is always a manual or scripted scale-up decision, not something autoscale rules do on their own.

def: Defining infrastructure in declarative template files (ARM, Bicep, or Terraform) that can be version-controlled, reviewed, and deployed repeatably, instead of manually clicking through the Azure portal.
eg: A design requirement for consistent, repeatable, auditable deployments across multiple environments is a strong signal that IaC belongs in the answer, not manual provisioning.

def: Network Watcher provides network-level diagnostic tools — IP flow verify (is a specific rule allowing or blocking a flow), flow logs (a record of the traffic flowing through a network; NSG flow logs are being retired on 30 September 2027 in favor of virtual network flow logs), and Connection Troubleshoot (an end-to-end reachability test) — for troubleshooting connectivity issues after a network is already built.
prompt: _____ provides network-level diagnostic tools — IP flow verify (is a specific rule allowing or blocking a flow), flow logs (a record of the traffic flowing through a network; NSG flow logs are being retired on 30 September 2027 in favor of virtual network flow logs), and Connection Troubleshoot (an end-to-end reachability test) — for troubleshooting connectivity issues after a network is already built.
eg: These are diagnostic tools for an existing network, not design-time governance controls — Azure landing zones and Azure Policy govern how a network gets built and configured in the first place.

def: A managed service that provides browser-based RDP or SSH access to a VM through the Azure portal over TLS, without ever requiring a public IP address on the target VM itself. In its standard deployment, Bastion lives in a dedicated subnet named AzureBastionSubnet within a VNet — commonly the hub VNet of a hub-and-spoke topology — and it is a complementary layer, not a replacement, for the NSG and Azure Firewall filtering that still protects those same VMs.
eg: Removing the VM's public IP closes one attack surface, but it doesn't make NSG rules optional — layered defense still applies with Bastion in place, not instead of it.

def: A shorthand for the range of ways a workload can move to the cloud, from least to most change: Rehost (lift-and-shift, minimal change), Refactor/re-platform (small optimizations, like moving to a managed database), Rearchitect (redesign for cloud-native scale), Rebuild (start over cloud-native), and Replace (swap it for a SaaS product instead of moving it at all). Azure Migrate typically drives the discovery and assessment that decides which of these five paths actually fits a given workload.
eg: A design question that only ever considers Rehost is missing the point of the framework — the 5 R's exist specifically because different workloads justify different amounts of change, and picking the same strategy for everything usually means either overpaying for cloud-native rework nobody needed, or under-investing in a workload that would have benefited from it.

term: Azure DNS: public zones vs. Private DNS zones
def: A public DNS zone hosts a domain's records for internet-wide resolution. A Private DNS zone resolves names only within one or more linked virtual networks, commonly used to give a private endpoint a friendly name that still resolves to its private IP address instead of its public one. This is the usual missing piece in a private endpoint design: without a linked Private DNS zone, a private endpoint's normal hostname won't automatically resolve to its private IP address.
eg: A private endpoint needs a linked Private DNS zone to make its private IP resolve automatically for VNet-based clients — without one, an application would have to be reconfigured to use the private endpoint's raw IP address directly.

def: Provides outbound-only internet connectivity for resources in a subnet through a shared set of static public IP addresses, avoiding the SNAT port exhaustion that can occur behind a Standard Load Balancer's outbound rules under heavy outbound connection volume.
eg: This solves outbound connectivity specifically — it doesn't provide any inbound path, which is a separate concern handled by a load balancer, Application Gateway, or Front Door.

term: Managed disks: Standard SSD vs. Premium SSD vs. Ultra Disk
def: Standard SSD suits dev/test or lighter, latency-tolerant workloads. Premium SSD targets production workloads needing consistent low latency and high IOPS, such as databases. Ultra Disk allows IOPS and throughput to be tuned independently of disk size, for the most demanding, latency-sensitive workloads.
eg: A requirement to adjust IOPS or throughput on the fly, independent of how much disk capacity is provisioned, is the specific signal for Ultra Disk over Premium SSD.

def: Manages a group of identical, load-balanced VMs as a single resource, automatically adding or removing instances based on autoscale rules — the VM-based equivalent of scaling out an App Service plan, but for IaaS workloads that need full OS control.
